doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

chapter: Basie band: origins, sound and style
title: How Basie became leader after Bennie Moten
summary: Hughes explains that after Moten died the band chose the easygoing Basie as front man.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: We are filming some interviews with some of the United States of America’s greatest jazz artists for Hamilton College. We are very privileged to have two members of the Count Basie Orchestra with us today. We have Frank Foster and Bill Hughes. My name is Mike Woods and I am a professor at Hamilton College, and my colleague, Monk Rowe, teaches saxophone also at the college. I’d like to start and ask you guys some questions about the Basie band and how it got started. Tell us how the Basie band kind of evolved out of the Benny Moten band.

Yeah, well, Basie was playing the piano in that band of course. And sometime down the line, Benny died. And the guys decided they wanted to get something going, and they formed a group, I think it was a small group at that point, but they decided that they wanted Basie to do the out front thing. And that’s really how he came to be the band leader. I don’t think he planned that at all, but it happened that all the guys liked him, you know, so they chose him to be the front man. That’s pretty generally how he got started being a band leader, of course it’s a little more involved than that. But he, I guess he had the type personality that all the guys figured they could live with that, you know, in leading the band.
Thought he was easy going, so he became a leader?
Yeah. And he stayed that way throughout his career. He was always easy going, you know, he was always “The Chief.” You’d ask him about being the band leader and he’d say “I’m just the piano player.”
